title: Anomaly and Outlier Detection
learning_outcomes: Explain anomaly and outlier detection and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of anomaly and outlier detection to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study anomaly and outlier detection in the context of unsupervised machine learning. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Anomaly and Outlier Detection matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Unsupervised methods seek structure when trusted target labels are not given. A visually appealing cluster is not automatically meaningful; assess stability and domain usefulness.

items.title: Statistical outlier detection
items.text: Define statistical outlier detection in relation to anomaly and outlier detection; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Isolation Forest
items.text: Work through isolation forest using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Local Outlier Factor
items.text: Check the edge cases for local outlier factor: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by anomaly and outlier detection. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.code:
basket = [{"bread", "milk"}, {"bread", "eggs"}, {"bread", "milk"}]
support = sum({"bread", "milk"}.issubset(b) for b in basket)/len(basket)
print("support bread+milk:", round(support, 2))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Association does not establish causation or guarantee a profitable recommendation.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Unsupervised methods seek structure when trusted target labels are not given.
